questions.q: What turns a plain workflow into a real quality gate, according to this lesson?
options: Pointing a real step at an actual test command, whose exit code becomes the workflow's result
Renaming the workflow file to include the word 'test'
Adding more echo statements to the workflow
Running the workflow on a bigger runner machine
questions.explain: The mechanism doesn't change — running a real test command (like dbt test) and using its exit code is what makes a workflow into a gate.

questions.q: What does a status check attach to?
options: A specific commit
The entire repository, with no way to trace it to a specific change
Only the repository owner's account
Nothing — status checks are purely informational with no attachment
questions.explain: Each workflow run's pass/fail result attaches directly to the commit that triggered it, visible in commit history and PR checks.

questions.q: What does a pull request's Checks tab show?
options: Every check across every commit on that PR, rolled into one place
Only the PR's title and description
A list of every contributor to the repository
Billing information for GitHub Actions usage
questions.explain: The Checks tab aggregates every workflow that ran against the PR's commits into a single view.

questions.q: What is required to make a failing status check actually block a merge?
options: Configuring a required status check on a branch protection rule
Nothing — any red X automatically blocks every merge by default
Manually emailing the repository admin every time
Deleting the failing commit
questions.explain: Without a required status check on a branch protection rule, a failing check is just a visual — the merge button stays clickable.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does a required status check beat relying on people to remember to run tests?
options: It doesn't get tired and doesn't make exceptions — it's a mechanism, not a policy someone can forget
People never forget to run tests, so this doesn't matter
Required status checks are optional and rarely used
It eliminates the need for tests altogether
questions.explain: A team relying on memory will eventually have someone forget, often right before a deadline — a required check enforces the rule mechanically.
